cases.title: A valid signature on a contradicted claim
cases.lesson: Origin and integrity do not establish content correspondence.
cases.declaredQuestion: What does the signature establish, and what must be tested separately?
cases.scenario: A sealed synthetic note says a tray contains five tiles. The author-stipulated tray contains three.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic tray contains exactly three tiles during the fixture.

expressions.form: The tray contains five tiles.
expressions.interpretationNote: The signature is stipulated valid only for origin and byte integrity.

claims.proposition: The synthetic tray contains five tiles during the fixture.

evidence.description: A stipulated valid signature binds the note bytes to the synthetic signer role.
The stipulated fixture comparison counts three tiles.

assessments.scope: Comparison with condition-1 inside this synthetic fixture only.
assessments.rationale: Five differs from the author-stipulated count of three.
assessments.limitations: This disposition is authored fixture behavior, not an oracle result or a judgment about the signer.

nonClaims: The signature does not make the assertion true.
The fixture does not classify or score the synthetic signer.

cases.title: Valid consequence from a contradicted premise
cases.lesson: Formal validity and premise correspondence are separate questions.
cases.declaredQuestion: Can an inference be valid while its empirical conclusion is contradicted?
cases.scenario: A calculation assumes four gates of width two, but the stipulated fixture has two such gates.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic wall has two gates and each gate is two units wide.

expressions.form: There are four gates; each is two units wide; therefore total gate width is eight units.
expressions.interpretationNote: The multiplication rule is interpreted under ordinary finite arithmetic.

claims.proposition: The synthetic wall has four gates.
Each gate is two units wide.
The total gate width is eight units.
Given claims 1 and 2, claim 3 follows by multiplication.
claims.scope: The declared premises and ordinary arithmetic rule.

evidence.description: The stipulated wall description contains two gates of two units each.

reasoning.rule: gate_count multiplied by width_per_gate equals total_gate_width
reasoning.structuralNote: The consequence is structurally valid under the declared premises.

assessments.scope: Only the declared inference form.
assessments.rationale: The multiplication conclusion follows from the two stated premises.
assessments.limitations: This assessment says nothing about whether either empirical premise obtains.

assessments.scope: The stipulated wall description only.
assessments.rationale: Two gates of width two yield four units, not four gates or eight units.
assessments.limitations: This fixture assessment does not invalidate the inference rule itself.

assessments.scope: Width of each stipulated gate only.
assessments.rationale: The two-unit width matches the author-stipulated condition.
assessments.limitations: Scoped support for this premise does not support the contradicted gate count.

nonClaims: Formal validity is not a global truth label.
A contradicted premise does not imply defective arithmetic.

cases.title: Supported conclusion reached by invalid reasoning
cases.lesson: A supported conclusion does not repair an invalid argument.
cases.declaredQuestion: Can a conclusion match the fixture while the offered reasoning fails?
cases.scenario: A box contains four red tokens. An argument concludes four solely because the box is square.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic box is square and contains four red tokens.

expressions.form: The box is square, therefore it contains four red tokens.
expressions.interpretationNote: No rule connecting squareness to token count is declared.

claims.proposition: The synthetic box is square.
The synthetic box contains four red tokens.
Claim 2 follows from claim 1 alone.

evidence.description: The stipulated fixture describes four red tokens.

reasoning.structuralNote: The premise does not entail the conclusion.

assessments.scope: The stipulated token count only.
assessments.rationale: The conclusion matches the author-stipulated token count.
assessments.limitations: Support for the conclusion does not support the offered inference.

assessments.scope: The declared inference form only.
assessments.rationale: No declared rule makes token count follow from box shape.
assessments.limitations: This assessment does not challenge the token count itself.

assessments.scope: Shape of the stipulated box only.
assessments.rationale: The box's squareness matches the author-stipulated condition.
assessments.limitations: Scoped support for box shape does not make token count follow from shape.

nonClaims: A matching conclusion does not validate the route used to reach it.
This fixture does not infer competence or intent.

cases.title: Two coherent stories selecting one event set
cases.lesson: Narrative coherence, selection, causal attribution and correspondence require separate inspection.
cases.declaredQuestion: How can two coherent stories differ without assigning one whole-story truth status?
cases.scenario: A synthetic square experiences a gate closure, crowd movement, a bell and later reopening. Two stories select different events and causes.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The four declared events occur in sequence; the fixture does not stipulate why the crowd moved.

expressions.form: The closure redirected the crowd; the bell merely marked the interval.
expressions.interpretationNote: This expression selects closure and movement as its causal frame.

expressions.form: The bell prompted the crowd to move while the closed gate shaped the route.
expressions.interpretationNote: This expression selects the bell as prompt and the gate as constraint.

claims.proposition: Within story A, gate closure caused the crowd movement.
claims.scope: The causal fragment extracted from story A.

claims.proposition: Within story B, the bell prompted the crowd movement.
claims.scope: The causal fragment extracted from story B.
claims.temporalQualifier: Across events 2 and 3 as narratively reordered.

evidence.description: The fixture stipulates event occurrence and sequence but no causal mechanism.

narratives.title: Closure and redirection
narratives.selectionRationale: Foreground the gate as the organizing constraint on movement.
narratives.coherenceNote: The selected sequence is internally intelligible.
narratives.fidelityNote: It includes three stipulated events and omits the bell.
narratives.correspondenceNote: The causal attribution is not stipulated by the fixture.

narratives.title: Bell and movement
narratives.selectionRationale: Foreground the audible marker as the organizing prompt for movement.
narratives.coherenceNote: The narrated order supplies an intelligible prompt structure.
narratives.fidelityNote: It includes three stipulated events, omits reopening and reorders bell before movement.
narratives.correspondenceNote: Neither the reordered chronology nor causal prompt is stipulated by the fixture.

assessments.scope: Story A selection, order and causal fragment only.
assessments.rationale: Selected events are stipulated, while the causal attribution is not.
assessments.limitations: No whole-story verdict and no narrator assessment is produced.

assessments.scope: Story B selection, order and causal fragment only.
assessments.rationale: Selected events are stipulated, while chronology is reordered and causation unstipulated.
assessments.limitations: Coherence is recorded separately from correspondence and fidelity.

nonClaims: Neither narrative receives a whole-story truth status.
Internal coherence does not establish causal correspondence.

cases.title: An official record corrected without erasing history
cases.lesson: Official status, correction lifecycle and empirical assessment are distinct.
cases.declaredQuestion: How can a correction repair reliance without turning lifecycle into a truth verdict?
cases.scenario: A synthetic office first publishes a count of twelve, then corrects it to seven while retaining the earlier record.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The stipulated fixture count is seven units.

expressions.form: Official bulletin one: the count is twelve.
expressions.interpretationNote: Official publication status is stipulated but not empirical accuracy.

expressions.form: Correction bulletin: replace twelve with seven for this count.
expressions.interpretationNote: The correction supersedes the active record while preserving the earlier bulletin.

claims.proposition: The fixture count is twelve units.
The fixture count is seven units.
claims.temporalQualifier: As asserted in the correction bulletin.

evidence.description: The author-stipulated count is seven.

assessments.scope: Bulletin one's count compared with condition-1.
assessments.rationale: Twelve differs from the stipulated count of seven.
assessments.limitations: Retraction, correction and source intent are not inferred from this disposition.

assessments.scope: Correction bulletin's count compared with condition-1.
assessments.rationale: Seven matches the stipulated fixture count.
assessments.limitations: Official status is not part of the comparison method.

lifecycleRecords.scope: Active count record for this fixture only.
lifecycleRecords.reason: The synthetic office issued an explicit replacement count.

nonClaims: Correction lifecycle is not itself a falsehood verdict.
Official publication does not establish empirical correspondence.

cases.title: An effective declaration with no physical power
cases.lesson: A performative can constitute institutional status without changing an empirical condition.
cases.declaredQuestion: What can an authorized declaration make institutionally so?
cases.scenario: A synthetic council validly declares a garden open while stipulated rain keeps its paths wet.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The council role has fixture authority to set the garden's open status at noon.
Rain leaves the synthetic garden paths wet at noon.

expressions.form: Under the garden rule, the garden is open from noon.
expressions.interpretationNote: The declaration operates only within the stipulated institutional rule.

expressions.form: Because the council opened the garden, the paths are dry.
expressions.interpretationNote: The expression improperly carries institutional force into a physical claim.

claims.proposition: The garden has open status from noon under the synthetic rule.
claims.temporalQualifier: From noon on the fixture date.

claims.proposition: The declaration caused the garden paths to be dry.
claims.scope: The physical paths in the synthetic garden.
claims.temporalQualifier: At noon on the fixture date.

evidence.description: The fixture grants the council role authority to set open status only.

assessments.scope: Felicity and authority under the invented garden rule only.
assessments.rationale: The declared role and procedure satisfy the fixture's institutional rule.
assessments.limitations: This method does not assess physical conditions or moral legitimacy.

assessments.scope: Physical path condition in this fixture only.
assessments.rationale: The stipulated paths remain wet after the declaration.
assessments.limitations: The empirical disposition does not undo the garden's institutional open status.

nonClaims: The atlas does not grant the council real authority.
Institutional validity is not empirical or moral validity.

cases.title: Relevant testimony receives less uptake
cases.lesson: Social uptake and evidential access are different; neither licenses a witness score.
cases.declaredQuestion: What changes when power affects who is heard rather than what was observed?
cases.scenario: A nearby anonymous observer reports a leak. A distant office report omits it and receives wider uptake.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: A synthetic pipe leaks and the anonymous observer role is nearby while the office role is remote.

expressions.form: I observed water escaping from the pipe.
expressions.interpretationNote: Anonymity is preserved and not converted into a credibility penalty.

expressions.form: The office record contains no leak entry, so no leak occurred.
expressions.interpretationNote: Archive silence is presented as event absence.

claims.proposition: The anonymous observer role reports seeing water escape from the pipe.
claims.scope: The one report and its declared access conditions.

claims.proposition: No leak occurred because the office archive contains no entry.
claims.scope: The synthetic pipe and office archive.

evidence.description: The observer role has direct stipulated proximity; the office role has only archive access.
The anonymous report receives one synthetic relay while the office report receives eight; relay count is social distribution only.

assessments.scope: Existence and access conditions of this testimony only.
assessments.rationale: The fixture contains the report, stipulates nearby access and separately records lower social distribution than the remote office report.
assessments.limitations: Relay count is not credibility or evidential strength; this does not score the witness, infer identity or establish all details of the reported event.

assessments.scope: The leak condition stipulated by condition-1.
assessments.rationale: The fixture stipulates a leak despite archive silence.
assessments.limitations: This illustrates archive incompleteness; it does not generalize to real testimony or institutions.

nonClaims: Anonymity is not low credibility.
The atlas never creates a witness or institution score.

cases.title: Five reports with one upstream assertion
cases.lesson: Source count and repetition do not establish independent support.
cases.declaredQuestion: How many independent observations exist when reports are syndicated?
cases.scenario: Five synthetic outlets repeat one upstream note without independent observation.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: All five reports derive from one upstream assertion and contain no independent observation.

expressions.form: Five sources independently confirm that the synthetic flag is raised.
expressions.interpretationNote: The expression claims independence, not merely five copies.

claims.proposition: Five independent observations support the flag assertion.
claims.scope: The provenance structure of the five synthetic reports.

evidence.description: Each of five report nodes points to the same upstream note.

assessments.scope: Independence of the five declared report nodes only.
assessments.rationale: The derivation graph contains one upstream assertion, not five independent observations.
assessments.limitations: The audit does not assess whether the underlying flag assertion corresponds to the fixture world.

nonClaims: Five copies are not five independent sources.
Source dependence is not a source-worth score.

cases.title: A fluent citation absent from the declared catalogue
cases.lesson: Plausible form does not establish source existence or support.
cases.declaredQuestion: What may be concluded when a citation-shaped string has no catalogue match?
cases.scenario: A synthetic model output cites an invented paper identifier that is absent from the closed fixture catalogue.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The closed fixture catalogue contains identifiers A-01 and A-02 but not Z-99.

expressions.form: The claim is established by Synthetic Review Z-99.
expressions.interpretationNote: No model runs; the text is a fixed fixture string.

claims.proposition: Identifier Z-99 exists in the declared fixture catalogue.

evidence.description: Exact lookup of Z-99 in the stipulated two-entry catalogue returns no entry.

assessments.scope: Existence of Z-99 in the declared catalogue only.
assessments.rationale: Z-99 is absent from the complete stipulated catalogue.
assessments.limitations: Catalogue absence outside this closed fixture is not inferred, and no model-wide reliability claim is made.

nonClaims: Citation shape is not source existence.
One fabricated fixture citation does not produce a model score.

cases.title: A refusal that asserts no hidden proposition
cases.lesson: Privacy-preserving non-disclosure is not deception or evidence of falsehood.
cases.declaredQuestion: What may be assessed when an expression is a refusal rather than an answer?
cases.scenario: A synthetic role declines to answer a private question; an observer claims the refusal proves a concealed assertion false.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The first expression is a refusal and contains no answer to the private question.

expressions.form: I decline to answer that private question.
expressions.interpretationNote: The refusal is not silently promoted into an answer.

expressions.form: The refusal proves the undisclosed answer would be false.
expressions.interpretationNote: This expression converts non-disclosure into an unsupported conclusion.

claims.proposition: The refusal establishes that an undisclosed answer would be false.

evidence.description: The expression is typed as REFUSAL with no answer claim.

assessments.scope: The inference from the refusal expression alone.
assessments.rationale: A refusal supplies no answer proposition from which falsehood follows.
assessments.limitations: The atlas does not infer private content, motive, belief or intent.

nonClaims: Silence or refusal is not an assertion of a false proposition.
No private state or intent is inferred.

cases.title: A self-referential sentence stopped at typed levels
cases.lesson: L0 claims, L1 assessments and L2 audits must not collapse into a fixed point.
cases.declaredQuestion: How should the atlas handle a sentence referring to its own assessment?
cases.scenario: A sentence says that no named method can support this very claim. The atlas refuses untyped self-adjudication.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The expression refers to assessment of its own claim and no object-language fixed-point semantics is declared.

expressions.form: This claim cannot be supported under any named method.
expressions.interpretationNote: The content mentions assessment, but the claim remains an L0 target.

claims.proposition: No named method can support this claim.
claims.scope: The sentence's own untyped assessment reference.

assessments.scope: Availability of a declared stratified interpretation method only.
assessments.rationale: The fixture declares no fixed-point semantics capable of adjudicating the self-reference.
assessments.limitations: OUTSIDE_NAMED_METHOD is a refusal to collapse levels, not a truth value for the sentence.

assessmentAudits.scope: Structural audit of L1 targeting and cycle absence only.
assessmentAudits.rationale: The L1 assessment targets only an L0 claim; the L2 audit targets only that L1 assessment.

nonClaims: The L1 disposition is not fed back as an L0 premise.
No paradox receives a fixed-point truth verdict.

cases.title: Unanimous repetition of a challenged claim
cases.lesson: Consensus and repetition do not establish correspondence.
cases.declaredQuestion: Does unanimous repetition change the relation between a claim and the declared fixture?
cases.scenario: Twelve synthetic voice tokens repeat that a marker is red; the stipulated marker is blue.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic marker is blue while twelve voice tokens repeat that it is red.

expressions.form: All twelve tokens say the marker is red, therefore it is red.
expressions.interpretationNote: Agreement is the stated basis.

claims.proposition: The synthetic marker is red.

evidence.description: Twelve identical assertion tokens are present.
The stipulated marker condition is blue.

assessments.scope: Marker colour in this fixture only.
assessments.rationale: Red conflicts with the stipulated blue condition; repetition is not used as a correspondence method.
assessments.limitations: No voice token is ranked or classified.

nonClaims: Unanimity is not an empirical instrument.
Consensus does not mint a truth state.

cases.title: Accurate fragments assembled into a misleading summary
cases.lesson: True-seeming fragments can mislead through selection and omission.
cases.declaredQuestion: How should selection be exposed without scoring an author or whole story?
cases.scenario: A summary reports the north indicator glowing and omits a simultaneous south alarm before claiming all systems are nominal.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The north indicator glows and the south alarm sounds at the same fixture time.

expressions.form: The north indicator is glowing; all systems are nominal.
expressions.interpretationNote: The second claim generalizes beyond the selected north event.

claims.proposition: The north indicator is glowing.
All synthetic systems are nominal.

evidence.description: The fixture contains both north glow and south alarm events.

narratives.title: North-only status summary
narratives.coherenceNote: The one-event summary is internally coherent.
narratives.fidelityNote: It selects the north event and omits the south alarm.
narratives.correspondenceNote: Its whole-system generalization conflicts with the omitted stipulated event.

narratives.title: Whole-panel counterstory
narratives.selectionRationale: Include both stipulated status events to test the north-only selection.
narratives.coherenceNote: The two-event frame is internally intelligible.
narratives.fidelityNote: It includes both stipulated status events and omits none.
narratives.correspondenceNote: It makes no whole-system nominal claim and supplies no causal attribution.

assessments.scope: North indicator condition only.
assessments.rationale: The north glow matches the stipulated event.
assessments.limitations: This scoped support cannot be promoted to whole-system status.

assessments.scope: Whole-system generalization and omitted event only.
assessments.rationale: A sounding alarm conflicts with the all-nominal generalization.
assessments.limitations: The assessment targets a claim fragment, not the summarizer's character or intent.

nonClaims: An accurate selected fact can accompany a challenged generalization.
Omission does not by itself establish deceptive intent.

cases.title: A once-supported claim carried past its time
cases.lesson: Temporal scope and currentness must be explicit.
cases.declaredQuestion: What changes when a supported record is reused after conditions change?
cases.scenario: A reservoir is stipulated at eight units at T1 and three at T2; a T1 report is presented as current at T2.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic reservoir level is eight at T1 and three at T2.

expressions.form: The reservoir level is eight units.
expressions.interpretationNote: The reused expression omits its original T1 qualifier.

expressions.form: At T2, the reservoir level is three units.
expressions.interpretationNote: The replacement expression declares its T2 qualifier.

claims.proposition: The reservoir level is eight units at T2.
claims.temporalQualifier: At T2 after reuse of a T1 report.

claims.proposition: The reservoir level is three units at T2.

evidence.description: The source report belongs to T1 while the target claim is scoped to T2.
The replacement record explicitly belongs to T2 and states three units.

assessments.scope: T2 currentness of the reused T1 expression only.
assessments.rationale: The fixture stipulates three at T2; the eight-unit value belongs to T1.
assessments.limitations: The assessment does not deny that the report matched T1.

assessments.scope: T2 currentness of the replacement expression only.
assessments.rationale: The replacement expression's T2 qualifier and value match the stipulated T2 condition.
assessments.limitations: Support is limited to the fixture's declared T2 record relation.

lifecycleRecords.reason: The T1 record is no longer current for T2.

nonClaims: A stale claim need not have always been unsupported.
The public atlas makes no runtime currentness claim.

cases.title: Attribution recorded while the metaphysical referent remains outside method
cases.lesson: A source-attribution record is not proof or disproof of its metaphysical or theological referent claim.
cases.declaredQuestion: What may Phase 0 establish about an invented source that advances a metaphysical claim?
cases.scenario: An invented scroll advances the proposition that an unobservable ember sustains the cosmos described by its discourse; the fixture stipulates only the source record.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The invented scroll contains the referent proposition; no method, observation, revelation authority or tradition is stipulated for adjudicating that proposition.
authorStipulatedConditions.scope: This closed invented source record only.

expressions.form: The invented Scroll of Ember advances: an unobservable ember sustains the cosmos described by this discourse.
expressions.interpretationNote: The attribution to the invented scroll and the referent proposition are represented as separate claims.

claims.proposition: The invented Scroll of Ember advances the referent proposition recorded in claim 2.
claims.scope: Existence and content attribution of the invented source record only.

claims.proposition: An unobservable ember sustains the cosmos described by the invented scroll's discourse.
claims.scope: The referent proposition itself, not merely its source attribution.

evidence.description: The fixed fixture bytes stipulate that the invented scroll advances the referent proposition.

assessments.scope: Whether the invented source record advances claim 2 only.
assessments.rationale: The fixed expression and stipulated source record contain the attributed proposition.
assessments.limitations: Support applies only to attribution; it supplies no proof, disproof, equation or authority concerning the referent proposition or any real tradition.

assessments.scope: Adjudication of the metaphysical referent proposition itself.
assessments.rationale: The named method checks attribution boundaries and declares no method for the referent proposition.
assessments.limitations: OUTSIDE_NAMED_METHOD is not proof, disproof, equivalence among traditions or a metaphysical verdict.

nonClaims: Recording that a source advances a claim does not establish the referent claim.
The atlas does not prove, disprove, rank or equate metaphysical or theological traditions.

cases.title: Genuine support and challenge remain unresolved
cases.lesson: Conflicting evidence may warrant contestability rather than forced closure.
cases.declaredQuestion: How does the atlas preserve a live conflict when no discriminating condition is stipulated?
cases.scenario: One synthetic trace bears in favor of a switch activation and another bears against it; neither is privileged by the fixture.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The fixture stipulates two intact conflicting traces and does not stipulate the switch state.

expressions.form: The switch was activated during interval Q.
expressions.interpretationNote: The target interval and switch are explicitly scoped.

claims.proposition: The synthetic switch was activated during interval Q.
claims.scope: The declared switch and interval Q.

evidence.description: Trace A bears in favor of activation under the named reading rule.
Trace B bears against activation under the same reading rule.

assessments.scope: The two stipulated traces under one reading rule.
assessments.rationale: One intact trace supports and one challenges, with no stipulated discriminator.
assessments.limitations: The contest is fixture- and method-scoped, not a global undecidability claim.

nonClaims: Conflict is preserved rather than averaged into a score.
Neither trace is ranked as a source.

cases.title: A metaphor protected from literal misclassification
cases.lesson: Genre and speech act must be interpreted before empirical testing.
cases.declaredQuestion: What is lost when a metaphor is silently converted into a literal claim?
cases.scenario: A poem says the archive is a river to evoke continuity through change.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The expression is declared poetic metaphor and not literal physical identity.
authorStipulatedConditions.scope: This closed fixture language practice only.

expressions.form: The archive is a river carrying yesterday into tomorrow.
expressions.interpretationNote: The declared comparison concerns continuity and change.

claims.proposition: The archive is compared to a river as a figure of continuity through change.

evidence.description: The fixture marks the expression as poetry and metaphor.

assessments.scope: Genre and declared non-literal speech act only.
assessments.rationale: The fixture explicitly declares the comparison as metaphorical.
assessments.limitations: The method does not adjudicate aesthetic worth, deeper meaning or literal physical correspondence.

nonClaims: The archive is not asserted to be a physical watercourse.
Poetry is not classified as deception.

cases.title: Fictional events without deceptive assertion
cases.lesson: Declared fiction and literal-world report occupy different regimes.
cases.declaredQuestion: Can an invented event be meaningful without being presented as empirical report?
cases.scenario: A declared fable describes a moonflower opening a locked sky gate.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The expression is openly declared an invented fable.
authorStipulatedConditions.scope: This closed fixture language practice only.

expressions.form: In the fable, the moonflower opens the locked sky gate.
expressions.interpretationNote: The in-story qualifier is explicit.

claims.proposition: Within the declared fable, the moonflower opens the sky gate.

evidence.description: The fixture labels the expression as invented fable narration.

assessments.scope: Fictional-world and genre framing only.
assessments.rationale: The claim is correctly scoped to the declared fable world.
assessments.limitations: No literal-world event, moral conclusion or aesthetic judgment is established.

nonClaims: The fable does not assert a literal sky gate exists.
Declared fiction is not a lie classification.

cases.title: An attributed propaganda label denied action authority
cases.lesson: Recording an institutional label must not become a misinformation flag, ranking or suppression command.
cases.declaredQuestion: What may Phase 0 record when an invented office labels a leaflet and asks for suppression?
cases.scenario: An invented office applies PROPAGANDA and MISINFORMATION labels to a synthetic leaflet and directs that it be removed.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The fixture stipulates that the office record contains the two labels and a removal directive, but declares no substantive classification method, legal process, rights analysis or action authority.

expressions.form: Office label: PROPAGANDA and MISINFORMATION. Remove the synthetic leaflet.
expressions.interpretationNote: The attributed label record and the requested suppression effect are represented separately.

claims.proposition: The invented office record applies PROPAGANDA and MISINFORMATION labels to the synthetic leaflet.
claims.scope: Presence and attribution of the invented label record only.

claims.proposition: The attributed labels authorize suppression of the synthetic leaflet.
claims.scope: The proposed removal effect and absent rights or legal process.

evidence.description: The fixed fixture bytes contain the office-attributed labels and requested removal.

assessments.scope: Presence and attribution of the invented office label record only.
assessments.rationale: The fixture stipulates that the office record contains the two attributed labels.
assessments.limitations: Support establishes only record attribution; it does not endorse the labels, flag content, rank a source or classify propaganda or misinformation.

assessments.scope: Whether the attributed labels authorize suppression or any downstream effect.
assessments.rationale: The Phase-0 method has no rights, legal, moderation, publication or enforcement process and grants no action authority.
assessments.limitations: OUTSIDE_NAMED_METHOD neither validates nor invalidates a separate lawful rights-respecting process; none is included here.

nonClaims: The atlas does not set a misinformation or propaganda flag.
No label, assessment or receipt authorizes censorship, suppression, moderation, publication change or enforcement.

cases.title: One source token with two declared readings
cases.lesson: Translation is a scoped mapping, not semantic identity.
cases.declaredQuestion: How should unresolved lexical alternatives be preserved?
cases.scenario: The invented source token luma can mean boundary-edge or protective-shelter; the sentence supplies no discriminator.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The invented lexicon permits EDGE and SHELTER readings for luma, with no contextual discriminator in the sentence.
authorStipulatedConditions.scope: This closed invented language practice only.

expressions.form: Luma remains after the storm.
expressions.interpretationNote: Both claim objects are candidate definitional readings, not simultaneous asserted identities.

claims.proposition: In this sentence, luma denotes a boundary-edge.
claims.scope: Candidate reading A in the invented language.

claims.proposition: In this sentence, luma denotes protective shelter.
claims.scope: Candidate reading B in the invented language.

evidence.description: The invented lexicon includes both readings and no priority rule.

assessments.scope: Selection between the two permitted readings for this sentence.
assessments.rationale: The named method finds both readings permitted and no declared discriminator.
assessments.limitations: The alternatives are preserved; no translation is crowned identical to the source token.

nonClaims: Translation does not establish semantic identity.
Ambiguity does not authorize silent selection.

cases.title: A first-person-seeming report without private-state inference
cases.lesson: The expression of experience and external-world correspondence require different access.
cases.declaredQuestion: What can be recorded about a phenomenal report without claiming access to private state?
cases.scenario: A synthetic subject role says a tone seems high; no external frequency or private-state access is stipulated.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The fixture contains the report expression but stipulates neither private experience nor an external tone measurement.

expressions.form: The tone seems high to me.
expressions.interpretationNote: The claim is scoped to apparent experience as expressed.

claims.proposition: The tone seems high to the synthetic subject role as expressed in the report.

evidence.description: The fixed fixture bytes contain the stated report.

assessments.scope: Presence and declared phenomenal framing of the expression only.
assessments.rationale: The expression record supports that the report is present and phenomenally framed.
assessments.limitations: No external frequency, private experience, sincerity, identity or intent is inferred.

nonClaims: The atlas has no access to private experience.
A phenomenal report is not an external measurement.

cases.title: A reasoned prediction that misses its horizon
cases.lesson: Ex-ante warrant and later outcome are different assessment targets.
cases.declaredQuestion: Does a missed outcome imply the forecast was irrational or deceptive?
cases.scenario: A fixed forecast predicts six arrivals by T2 from declared assumptions; the fixture later stipulates four arrivals.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The forecast declares assumptions at T1 and the fixture stipulates four arrivals at T2.

expressions.form: Under assumptions A and B, six arrivals are predicted by T2.
expressions.interpretationNote: The assumptions and T2 horizon are explicit.

claims.proposition: Six synthetic arrivals will occur by T2 under assumptions A and B.
claims.scope: The declared fixture process and assumptions.
claims.temporalQualifier: Forecast at T1 for horizon T2.

evidence.description: The stipulated T2 outcome contains four arrivals.

assessments.scope: Numeric outcome at the stipulated T2 horizon only.
assessments.rationale: The forecasted six differs from the stipulated outcome of four.
assessments.limitations: Outcome mismatch does not determine ex-ante rationality, competence, sincerity or intent.

nonClaims: A failed prediction is not a liar classification.
Forecast quality is not aggregated into a score.

cases.title: Two counterfactual models without an intervention
cases.lesson: Counterfactual claims are model-relative and not direct observations.
cases.declaredQuestion: What can be said when two declared models disagree about an unperformed alternative?
cases.scenario: Model A predicts a level drop if a valve opened; model B predicts no change. The valve remains closed.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The valve remains closed; models A and B have different declared response rules and no discriminator is stipulated.

expressions.form: If the valve had opened, the level would have fallen.
expressions.interpretationNote: The claim belongs to model A's declared alternative world.

claims.proposition: Under the alternative where the valve opens, the synthetic level falls.
claims.scope: The declared alternative and competing models.
claims.temporalQualifier: At the unperformed fixture intervention horizon.

evidence.description: Model A predicts a fall and model B predicts no change; no intervention occurs.

assessments.scope: The two declared response rules without an intervention or discriminator.
assessments.rationale: The named comparison records incompatible model outputs but has no stipulated basis to privilege one.
assessments.limitations: The unperformed alternative is not treated as an observed world condition.

nonClaims: A model output is not direct observation of an alternative world.
The atlas does not rank the competing models.

cases.title: A factual observation that does not supply an ought
cases.lesson: Normative conclusions require declared normative premises and affected commitments.
cases.declaredQuestion: Can a congestion measurement alone establish what ought to be done?
cases.scenario: A synthetic gate is congested. A statement concludes a second gate ought to open without declaring a normative premise.

authorStipulatedConditions.statement: The synthetic north gate is congested; the fixture declares no priority, duty, cost, consent or safety premise.

expressions.form: The north gate is congested, therefore the south gate ought to be opened.
expressions.interpretationNote: The conclusion is normative even though the only declared premise is empirical.

claims.proposition: The south gate ought to be opened because the north gate is congested.
claims.scope: The invented gate choice and unnamed affected interests.

evidence.description: The fixture stipulates congestion but no normative bridge premise.

assessments.scope: Presence of declared normative bridge premises only.
assessments.rationale: Congestion is stipulated, but no duty, priority, consent, safety or cost premise connects it to the proposed directive.
assessments.limitations: The atlas does not recommend whether either gate should open and authorizes no action.

nonClaims: An empirical observation does not silently derive an ought.
No gate action is recommended or authorized.
